claims.text: In-situ formation of a thin, stable oxide layer is the dominant factor controlling the wear performance of high-entropy-alloy protective coatings.
A stable oxide layer reduces metal-to-metal contact and wear by accommodating stress.
A stable oxide layer lowers friction during sliding.
The CuMoTaWV refractory HEA film used as the model initial state is nanocrystalline.
The CuMoTaWV refractory HEA film has a BCC solid-solution structure.
Solid-solution hardening contributes to the initial coating's mechanical state.
Grain-boundary strengthening contributes to the initial coating's mechanical state.
Controlled annealing or increased oxygen partial pressure will promote a continuous, well-adherent oxide film on the coating.
CuMoTaWV coatings can be subjected to sliding-wear tests at room temperature and 300 °C against a standardized counter-body.
The relevant structural mediator is a nanometer-scale surface oxide such as CuO or a spinel phase.
Tribo-oxidation rapidly develops a protective oxide film under sliding conditions.
The tribo-oxide reduces direct contact between asperities, thereby lowering friction coefficient and wear rate.
The oxide film stabilizes the surface and mitigates mechanical degradation.
Pre-oxidized coatings or coatings allowed to oxidize in situ will have significantly lower wear rates than coatings tested under oxidation-suppressing inert conditions.
Pre-oxidized coatings or coatings allowed to oxidize in situ will have lower coefficients of friction than coatings tested under oxidation-suppressing inert conditions.
The proposed oxide-controlled mechanism should dominate from room temperature to approximately 300 °C when oxygen availability supports stable oxide formation without detrimental over-oxidation.
The protective effect may fail at low temperatures with insufficient oxidation or at high temperatures where oxide layers degrade.

If a minimally oxidized control shows similar or lower wear rate and friction coefficient than an oxidized coating under otherwise identical conditions, oxide-film formation is not the primary mechanism governing wear performance.
